summary: NASA’s data tools can plot how rainfall, heat or groundwater change over time, but they leave the hardest question open: is that trend real, or just random ups and downs? Kuch Toh Gadbad Hai (“something’s not right here”) is a web and Android app that turns anyone into a data detective. Answer three short questions, pick a place on a map or 3D globe, and the app shows the time series, the rate of change, and a plain verdict: Confirmed, Likely, or Not proven. Each verdict is backed by a t-test, the Mann-Kendall test and a confidence interval, shown side by side. When a trend is not yet proven, the app says how many more years of data would be needed. It also investigates “mirror cases”: regions where the same variable moves in opposite directions, and tests whether one cause explains both. It works in English and Hindi, in simple or scientist mode.
details:
The gap we address
NASA tools such as Giovanni and AppEEARS can already draw a time series for almost any variable. What they leave open is the question people care about: is this trend real, or could ordinary year-to-year variation produce it by chance? Kuch Toh Gadbad Hai (“something’s not right here”, a detective’s catchphrase in India) is built to answer that question for anyone, anywhere on Earth.

What it does and how it works

  1. Ask: three short questions (what worries you, where, which season) lead to matching variables, each with a one-line definition.
  2. Look: a flat map or 3D globe shows where the variable is rising or falling. Tap a point, choose a region type (desert, rain forest, estuary, large city) or draw your own region.
  3. Test: the app builds the time series, removes the seasonal cycle, and reports the rate of change per decade with three checks side by side: a t-test on the fitted line, the Mann-Kendall test, and a 95% confidence interval. Monthly data also get the Seasonal Mann-Kendall test.
  4. Verdict: one stamp in plain words: Confirmed, Likely, or Not proven. If not proven, the app estimates how many more years of data would be needed.

How it is creative

  • It tests causes, not only trends. The challenge notes that one process can push a variable up in one region and down in another. Our “mirror cases” find such pairs and test suspects such as El Niño, the Indian Ocean Dipole and global warming against both regions. The verdict can be “same cause”, “different culprit” or “not proven”.
  • It completes NASA’s own tools. A file exported from Giovanni, AppEEARS or NOAA Climate Data Online can be dropped in and judged by the same method.
  • It audits itself. A cherry-pick check repeats the test for every start and end year. An “alibi” check flags jumps that coincide with instrument changes. We publish our measured false-alarm rate.
  • It teaches by play. In “Can you beat the test?” users guess which of ten charts hide a real trend, and learn why eyes alone are not enough.

Results on real data
14 datasets, 7 case files and 30 cities are live. On noisy test series, an uncorrected test raised false alarms 26 to 31% of the time; our corrected test, 8 to 9%. Our Arctic September sea-ice trend is -11.86% per decade; the published value is -11.9%. GRACE satellites show land water storage changing significantly over 40% of land. In north-west India, where groundwater is falling, the detective cleared rainfall and climate drivers and points to a local cause.

Benefits and intended impact
Students learn what “significant” means by doing it. Journalists and local officials can check a claim before repeating it. Farmers and residents can see 40 years of heat, rain and soil moisture for their own town, in English or Hindi. Scientists can open Scientist mode and reproduce every number. The aim is fewer false alarms and fewer missed warnings in public conversations about a changing Earth.

Tools and data
Python (xarray, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, earthaccess) for the data pipeline. Flutter for one codebase on web and Android. Firebase Hosting, Firestore and AI Logic (Gemini). Data: NASA GISTEMP, GRACE/GRACE-FO, GLDAS, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2, NASA POWER, with NOAA and NSIDC indices. It runs entirely on free tiers.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty over drama: “Not proven” is a valid answer, and we show it.
  • Year-to-year memory in climate data inflates significance, so our tests correct for it.
  • Thousands of map cells tested at once produce false positives, so maps use false-discovery control.
  • Accessibility: plain words first, numbers on request, two languages, phone to desktop.
  • Limits we state openly: trends are linear, a statistical link is not proof of cause, and MODIS, OMI and AIRS enter through file upload, not as built-in maps.

Use of AI
Code, documentation, interface design and our presentation script were written with an AI assistant (Anthropic Claude) and reviewed by the team. In the app, plain-language notes and summaries come from Google Gemini, with Groq- and OpenRouter-hosted open models as back-ups, and are always labelled as AI. The short opening video was generated with Google Gemini and carries an "AI-generated" label. The demo video's voice-over was generated with ElevenLabs. No verdict, number, map or chart comes from AI. Sample files are synthetic and labelled.
